## Proof

**Claim.** The only entire function satisfying $f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=\tfrac{1}{n^{2}}$ for every positive integer $n$ is $f(z)=z^{2}$.

**Existence.** The function $f(z)=z^{2}$ is entire (a polynomial), and for every positive integer $n$,
$$f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^{2}=\tfrac{1}{n^{2}}.$$
So $f(z)=z^{2}$ is a valid solution.

**Uniqueness.** Let $g$ be any entire function with $g\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=\tfrac{1}{n^{2}}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. Define
$$h(z):=g(z)-z^{2}.$$
Since $g$ is entire and $z^{2}$ is entire, $h$ is entire. Moreover, for every positive integer $n$,
$$h\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=g\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)-\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^{2}=\tfrac{1}{n^{2}}-\tfrac{1}{n^{2}}=0.$$
Thus the set $Z:=\{z:h(z)=0\}$ contains the infinite set $\left\{\tfrac{1}{n}:n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\right\}$. This set has an accumulation point, namely $0$, and $0$ lies in the domain of $h$ (which is all of $\mathbb{C}$).

By the **identity theorem** for holomorphic functions: if two holomorphic functions on a connected open set agree on a set that has an accumulation point within that set, then they are identical. Applying this to $h$ and the zero function (both entire, agreeing on $\{1/n\}$ which accumulates at $0\in\mathbb{C}$), we conclude
$$h\equiv 0,$$
and therefore
$$g(z)=z^{2}\quad\text{for all }z\in\mathbb{C}.$$

**Conclusion.** The unique entire function satisfying the given condition is

$$\boxed{f(z)=z^{2}}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
